clue.text: Regularly strip away lustre when breaking tektite

indicators.note: something breaking falls apart and its pieces end up in a new order
regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter of the phrase that follows is kept

parts.note: the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters of the phrase
taken as written

explanation.surface: Polishing a glassy meteorite stone: the shine is stripped off once it cracks.
explanation.walkthrough: The kept letters of 'strip away' join LUSTRE and the ten letters are rearranged into AUSTRALITE.
explanation.definitionFit: Australites are a type of tektite, the natural glass bodies formed by meteorite impacts and found across southern Australia.

clue.text: The most modern in a couple of ways?

wordplay.note: two compass directions, NE (north-east) followed by WEST

explanation.surface: Musing that the very latest thing might be new in two different senses.
explanation.walkthrough: Ways here are compass directions: NE and WEST, the couple, sit side by side. The question mark flags this reading of 'ways'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something newest is the latest, most recent or up to date of its kind, the superlative of new.

clue.text: Potentate supporting American state's Sikh centre?

indicators.note: in a down entry, a part that supports another sits underneath it, so the ruler comes last

parts.note: standard abbreviation for American
Rhode Island, the US state's postal code
a tsar is an absolute ruler

explanation.surface: A powerful ruler propping up an American state, with a hint at religion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supporting' places the ruler below the other two parts in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Amritsar, in Punjab, is home to the Golden Temple, the holiest shrine of the Sikh faith.

clue.text: Short fit relative

indicators.note: something short is cut down, so the final letter of the term is lopped off

parts.note: grand mal is a severe epileptic seizure

explanation.surface: A brief tantrum thrown by a family member.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fit' looks like an adjective meaning healthy but is a seizure, GRAND MAL, docked of its L.
explanation.definitionFit: A grandmother is a family member, two generations up, and grandma is the familiar name for her.

clue.text: Husband into odd side of barn dance

indicators.note: one letter is put into the middle of the other parts

parts.note: rum is a dated word for strange

indicators.note: a side is one half, so only the front half of the following word is used

parts.note: the first half of the word
standard abbreviation for husband

explanation.surface: A husband dragged onto the floor at a country barn dance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Barn dance' reads as one thing, but 'barn' is split off for wordplay. Rum, meaning odd or strange, is old British slang.
explanation.definitionFit: The rhumba is a Cuban ballroom dance, also spelled rumba, with lively hip movements.

clue.text: Eminence of pound dropping one place in range

indicators.note: the dropped letter only falls a single position, so it goes back in just one step further down
dropping a thing means letting it fall from its spot at the start of the word

parts.note: latitude is scope or range for freedom of action
L, from Latin libra, is the symbol for a pound

explanation.surface: A heavyweight coin slipping down a mountain range from its lofty perch.
explanation.walkthrough: In LATITUDE the pound sign starts the word; moving it down one place swaps it with the A that follows.
explanation.definitionFit: An eminence is a high piece of ground, and altitude is height above sea level, so both describe elevation.

clue.text: Pool nothing more

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a lake or pond
second meaning: an adjective for something that is only what it is

explanation.walkthrough: The words read like a shrug about a pond, but they are two separate meanings of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is a poetic noun for a lake and an adjective meaning simply, being no greater than stated.

clue.text: Underground bar making a comeback, ending in failure

indicators.note: coming back means going the other way, so the word is read from right to left

parts.note: bar and but both mean except

indicators.note: the ending of the next word supplies only its last letter

parts.note: final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A pub on the underground scene staging a comeback that ends in failure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bar' looks like a pub but means except, as in 'all bar one'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Tube is the everyday name for the London Underground railway network.

clue.text: When reported, mother must call on old prison

indicators.note: reported speech is something said out loud, so the words are judged by how they sound

parts.note: MA for mother, SHALL for must, SEE for call on, as in visiting

explanation.surface: A son told that his mum must visit someone in an old jail.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'see' someone is to call on them. In non-rhotic British speech MAR sounds like MA.
explanation.definitionFit: The Marshalsea was a notorious debtors' prison in Southwark, London, where Dickens's father was held.

clue.text: America again exposed monstrous European citizen

parts.note: standard abbreviation
then can mean besides or again, as in 'but then'

indicators.note: something exposed has had its covering stripped off, so the outer letters go

parts.note: GIANT means monstrous; its inside letters are kept

explanation.surface: A bombastic story of an America unmasked yet again as a monster.
explanation.walkthrough: GIANT, meaning monstrous, loses its outer letters, leaving the middle.
explanation.definitionFit: An Athenian is a native or resident of Athens, the Greek capital, so a citizen of a European city.

clue.text: Wounded setter guarding train depot's entrance

indicators.note: a guard surrounds what it protects, so one piece encloses another

parts.note: the setter refers to themselves as me
to train a gun is to aim it

indicators.note: the entrance of a word is its opening letter

parts.note: first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A crossword compiler, injured while standing guard at a railway depot gate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Train' suggests the railway but is a verb meaning point a weapon.
explanation.definitionFit: To maim is to injure severely, so someone maimed has been badly hurt, often permanently.

clue.text: Bum quaffing new port

indicators.note: quaffing is drinking down, so the outer word takes the other inside it

parts.note: the nates are the buttocks, in anatomical Latin
standard abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: A tramp downing some freshly bought port wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Port' looks like the drink being quaffed, but it is a harbour city. In British slang a bum is the backside.
explanation.definitionFit: Nantes is a city on the Loire in western France, historically a major river port and shipbuilding centre.

clue.text: I'm guilty of a choice about hosting nude show

indicators.note: a host takes a guest in, so one part goes within the other
turning about means facing the other way, so the preceding words are read backwards

parts.note: taken as written
a plum job is a choice one

indicators.note: a nude thing has nothing on its outside, so the word loses its first and last letters

parts.note: TEACH means show, as in show someone how; its middle is kept

explanation.surface: Someone owning up to choosing a strip show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nude show' reads as a striptease but means TEACH stripped of its edges.
explanation.definitionFit: Mea culpa is Latin for 'my fault', said as an admission of blame or error.

clue.text: Pin bulk of credit crunches on former financial guide

indicators.note: crunching something smashes it up and the bits settle in a new order
the bulk is most but not all, so the last letter is cut

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
an ex is a former partner

explanation.surface: Blaming the credit crunch on a former financial indicator.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Credit crunch' is a familiar phrase, but here 'crunches' signals the rearrangement of PIN and CREDI.
explanation.definitionFit: A price index tracks the changing cost of goods over time, a standard measure that guides economic decisions.

clue.text: Tradesmen partly reversed across red light

indicators.note: reversed means read in the opposite direction, right to left
partly means only a portion, so the letters are a run lifted from inside the words

parts.note: a run of letters read backwards from the end of light to the end of across

explanation.surface: Workmen who backed up through a red traffic light.
explanation.definitionFit: Gilders are craftsmen who apply thin gold leaf to frames, furniture and books.

clue.text: Rob unlicensed taxi mainly in republic

indicators.note: mainly means most of it, so the last letter is cut

parts.note: to do someone is slang for rob or cheat them
a minicab cannot be hailed in the street like a licensed cab

explanation.surface: Mugged by a rogue cab driver while abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: A minicab is a British private-hire car that must be booked rather than hailed, unlike a licensed black cab.
explanation.definitionFit: Dominica is an island republic in the Caribbean, independent from Britain since 1978.

clue.text: Appeared as a swelling in fruit

parts.note: to rise is to swell up, as dough does
both mean fashionable

explanation.surface: A lump that showed up in a piece of fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like it places the swelling inside the fruit, but it means trendy.
explanation.definitionFit: A rosehip is the red seed pod that forms on a rose bush after flowering, used for syrup and tea.

clue.text: Officially noted by coroner: unexpectedly died

indicators.note: an unexpected outcome is out of the usual order, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
standard abbreviation for died

explanation.surface: A coroner's formal verdict of an unexpected death.
explanation.definitionFit: Something on record has been formally documented and acknowledged publicly as the official position.

clue.text: Trouble about entering boring item on advanced CV

indicators.note: in a down entry one piece placed on another sits directly above it
what enters goes inside, so one piece sits within the next

parts.note: a drill bit bores holes

indicators.note: turning about means facing the other way, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: ado is fuss or bother
standard abbreviation, as in A level

explanation.surface: Fretting about a dull detail in a job applicant's high-level CV.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boring' looks like tedious but means drilling holes.
explanation.definitionFit: Biodata is a person's biographical details, a term used in place of a résumé in some countries.

clue.text: Desperate northern miner swinging both ways for money overseas

indicators.note: someone desperate is in a frantic state, so these letters lose their order

parts.note: standard abbreviation
taken as written
bi is short for bisexual

explanation.surface: A destitute pit worker from the north, open to anything for cash abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swinging both ways' suggests movement but is slang for bisexual.
explanation.definitionFit: The renminbi is the official currency of China, so it is the money used in a foreign country.

clue.text: One wanting masseur examined by auditors?

indicators.note: auditors are listeners, so the word is judged by its sound rather than its spelling

parts.note: a masseur kneads muscles

explanation.surface: A masseur hopefully inspected by accountants checking the books.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Auditors' looks like accountants, but here means people who hear.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who needs something lacks it and wants it, so a needer is a person in want.

clue.text: Expelling all adults from area, a great sorrow emerges

indicators.note: expelling every one means throwing out each occurrence of that letter from the phrase

parts.note: A is the old film certificate for adults
taken as written

explanation.surface: Grown-ups cleared out of a district, leaving great sadness behind.
explanation.walkthrough: Every A goes from 'area, a great'; what is left reads straight off in order.
explanation.definitionFit: Regret is a feeling of sadness or disappointment over something done or lost, a close synonym of sorrow.

clue.text: Probe excessively, intermittently moving up

indicators.note: in a down entry going up means reading from bottom to top

parts.note: over the top

indicators.note: intermittently means on and off, so only every other letter is kept

parts.note: second, fourth and sixth letters

explanation.surface: Investigating too keenly, with progress made only in fits and starts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Probe' looks like a verb meaning investigate but is the name of a spacecraft.
explanation.definitionFit: Giotto was a European Space Agency probe sent to study Halley's Comet in 1986, named after the painter.

clue.text: Heavyweight punches champion immediately

indicators.note: a punch lands inside its target, so one word goes in the other

parts.note: an ace is an expert or champion
a ton is a heavy weight

explanation.surface: A heavyweight boxer landing a blow on the title holder straight away.
explanation.walkthrough: The boxing picture misleads: the heavyweight is just a weight.
explanation.definitionFit: Both mean without any delay, straight away, right now.

clue.text: Concern over pitfall

indicators.note: turning something over flips it, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: to have a part in something is to have a concern in it

explanation.surface: Worry about some hidden danger.
explanation.definitionFit: A pitfall is a hidden danger or snare, literally a covered pit for catching animals.

clue.text: Bond villain's rent included in retrograde old type of payment

indicators.note: something included in another sits inside it
retrograde means moving backwards, so the words are read from the end

parts.note: standard abbreviation
cash on delivery
rent as the past tense of rend, torn

explanation.surface: A villain's rent money tucked into an outdated way of paying.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rent' is not money but the past participle of rend, to tear.
explanation.definitionFit: Doctor No is the title villain of the first James Bond film and Ian Fleming's sixth Bond novel.

clue.text: City centre has developed next to motorway

indicators.note: next to means right beside, so the pieces are joined end to end

parts.note: British motorways are numbered with M, as in the M1

indicators.note: something developed has grown into a new shape, so the letters are reorganised

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A city centre has grown up beside the motorway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'City centre' reads as a single phrase, but 'City' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Manchester is a major English city in the north-west, famed for its industry and football clubs.

clue.text: Row concerning sex from behind?

indicators.note: starting from behind means reading from the back, right to left

parts.note: re means about or concerning
it is a coy word for sex

explanation.surface: An argument about sex, with a cheeky hint at the position.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Row' suggests a quarrel, but it means a line, as of seats.
explanation.definitionFit: A tier is one of a series of rows or levels placed one above another, as of seats.
